newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh T-bill yields seen easing further - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh T-bill yields seen easing further - dealers.

text.p: Yields on Kazakh Treasury bills (GKOs) could fall further at auctions next week due to central bank efforts to cut yields on liquidity notes and increased activity by foreign investors, dealers said on Friday.
The National Bank is offering 250 million tenge of 12-month bills on Monday and 620 million tenge of three-month GKOs on Tuesday.

Average yields on six-month GKOs eased to 30.39 percent annual at an auction on Monday from 30.81 on January 20, while the yield on three-month GKOs edged down to 25.22 percent on Tuesday from 25.40 percent on January 29.
"The National Bank has obviously decided to bring down yields on its notes, and investors could prefer to put money in GKOs," Oleg Tsurkan, chief treasurer at ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan, told Reuters.
The central bank holds regular auctions of its high-yield seven- and 14-day notes to sterilise the money in circulation and support the national tenge currency.

At the last auction of seven-day notes on Thursday the National Bank cut the maximum yield to 32.44 percent from 53.58 percent a week earlier. The average yield was unchanged at 26.13 percent annual, but yields are likely to fall further.

"Most probably, local banks were bidding for higher yields having in mind previous auctions when the central bank satisfied all demands with a single wish -- to keep the tenge stable," said Irshat Shalin of Alfa Bank Kazakhstan.
At the last auction the central bank offered notes worth a total of two billion tenge, but sold paper worth only 683.4 million. Bids totalled 1.4 billion tenge.

"The central bank has obviously decided it is free not to place a whole issue, but just part of it -- in line with current market conditions... Investors might start putting more in GKOs, and this could bring down their yields," Tsurkan said.
Foreign investors -- more accustomed to working in a low inflation, low yield environment -- are becoming more active on the Kazakh market, dealers say.

"Foreigners are still allowed to buy only 15 to 30 percent of each GKO issue. But they are attracted by this market because yields on Kazakh paper are much higher than the usual 5-6 percent paid on similar securities in the West," Tsurkan said.
